author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Emma Woodhouse, being exceptionally well-endowed by both nature and fortune with a handsome countenance, a clever mind, and an abundance of wealth, had managed to spend nearly twenty-one years in this world without encountering anything substantial enough to cause her genuine distress.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: She had the fortune, or perhaps the misfortune, to be the youngest daughter of a father whose affection was entirely unchecked by discipline. Her mother having died too early to leave more than a shadowy recollection, her education had been entrusted to a governess whose indulgence proved little inferior to a parent's.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: For sixteen years, Miss Taylor had resided in Mr. Woodhouse's family; but the mildness of her temper having long since eroded any semblance of pedagogical authority, the relationship had ripened into the intimacy of sisters, leaving Emma entirely at liberty to follow her own inclinations.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: The true evils of Emma's situation were, indeed, the unchecked power of having her own way, and a disposition to think rather too well of her own abilities; yet these disadvantages were so pleasantly disguised that they by no means appeared to her in the light of misfortunes.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Sorrow came at last, though in no very disagreeable form, when Miss Taylor married. It was on the evening of this very wedding day, with the guests departed and her father retreating into his customary post-prandial slumber, that Emma was first left to the melancholy contemplation of her own loss.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: The match held every promise of felicity, Mr. Weston being a man of unexceptionable character and easy fortune; yet there was a black morning’s work for Emma in the realization that the daily, hourly comfort of an intelligent and perfectly unreserved companion was gone forever.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: How she was to bear the change was a question of some anxiety; for though Mrs. Weston was but half a mile distant, Emma was acutely aware of the difference between a friend in the neighborhood and a friend in the house, especially as her father's conversational powers were notably deficient.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Mr. Woodhouse's habits as a valetudinarian, lacking both mental and physical vigor, effectively doubled the disparity of their ages; and while his amiable temper secured universal affection, his talents could never have recommended him as an engaging companion.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Her sister, being established in London some sixteen miles distant, was removed far beyond the convenience of daily intercourse; leaving Emma to anticipate many a long, unbroken autumn evening before the Christmas holidays might afford her the relief of society.

author: Jane Austen
